introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics 3 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Time allowed: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. For your guidance the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.
enonce_intro_markdown:
A particle $P$ moves on the curve with polar equation $r = e^{\theta}$, where $(r, \theta)$ are the polar coordinates referred to a fixed pole, in such a way that the transverse component of its acceleration is always zero.

Show that

questions.corrige_markdown:
In polar coordinates the transverse component of the acceleration is

$$a_\theta = r\ddot{\theta} + 2\dot{r}\dot{\theta} = \frac{1}{r}\frac{d}{dt}\left(r^2\dot{\theta}\right)$$

(Indeed $\dfrac{d}{dt}(r^2\dot\theta) = 2r\dot r\dot\theta + r^2\ddot\theta = r\,(r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta)$.)

The transverse component is always zero, and $r > 0$, so

$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(r^2\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right) = 0\ \Rightarrow\ r^2\frac{d\theta}{dt} = k,\quad k\ \text{constant}$$

Differentiate $r = e^{\theta}$ with respect to $t$:

$$\frac{dr}{dt} = e^{\theta}\frac{d\theta}{dt} = r\,\frac{d\theta}{dt}$$

From part (i), $\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \dfrac{k}{r^2}$, so

$$\frac{dr}{dt} = r\cdot\frac{k}{r^2} = \frac{k}{r}$$

as required.

questions.enonce_markdown: Hence, when $r = a$, find the speed of $P$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The radial and transverse components of the velocity are $\dot r$ and $r\dot\theta$. When $r = a$:

$$\dot r = \frac{k}{a},\qquad r\dot\theta = r\cdot\frac{k}{r^2} = \frac{k}{a}$$

$$\text{speed}^2 = \dot r^2 + (r\dot\theta)^2 = \frac{k^2}{a^2} + \frac{k^2}{a^2} = \frac{2k^2}{a^2}$$

$$\text{speed} = \frac{\sqrt{2}\,k}{a}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Hence, when $r = a$, find the radial component of the acceleration of $P$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The radial component of the acceleration is $a_r = \ddot r - r\dot\theta^2$.

**First term.** Since $\dot r = \dfrac{k}{r}$,

$$\ddot r = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{k}{r}\right) = -\frac{k}{r^2}\,\dot r = -\frac{k}{r^2}\cdot\frac{k}{r} = -\frac{k^2}{r^3}$$

**Second term.** $r\dot\theta^2 = r\left(\dfrac{k}{r^2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{k^2}{r^3}$.

$$a_r = -\frac{k^2}{r^3} - \frac{k^2}{r^3} = -\frac{2k^2}{r^3}$$

When $r = a$:

$$a_r = -\frac{2k^2}{a^3}$$

The radial component has magnitude $\dfrac{2k^2}{a^3}$ and is directed towards the pole.
